extracted.intended_audience: employers, immigration attorneys, labor advocates, and other stakeholders commenting on or affected by USCIS H-1B cap selection rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Final rule and responses-to-comments establishing a wage-level weighted H-1B registration selection process and the analytical, procedural, and transparency standards DHS used to justify and implement the rule. Includes DHS reasoning on comment-period adequacy, regulatory analysis, data publication, and operational modeling choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative complexity and operational burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters: the current system is already difficult to navigate and the proposed rule would make the system more confusing and add unnecessary complexity and burden; the weighted selection process would be far more complex, resource intensive, and lead to adjudication delays, inconsistent adjudications, and possibly filing errors or erroneous rejections; increased complexity would increase costs for government, petitioners, and taxpayers; risk of technical system errors and unfair rejections. DHS response: does not agree the weighted selection process adds unnecessary complexity or confusion; USCIS does not adjudicate the registration; adjudicators will need training and extra review time but DHS does not anticipate unnecessary delays; rule does not impact current H-1B filing or registration fees; USCIS confident system will be operable for FY 2027 and will take remedial measures if inoperable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proposed selection changes for required training, adjudicative time, likely processing delays, fee impacts, and technical operability; DHS treats administrative burden claims by (a) clarifying which processes are affected (registrations vs petitions), (b) noting fee review is biennial, and (c) reserving remedial operational steps if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of weighting scheme and selection outcome transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters requested publishing the exact weighting scheme in advance (including any caps), 'final technical guidance', and selection outcomes by wage level, degree type, employer size, NAICS code, and geography so stakeholders can validate impacts and detect misuse. DHS response: regulations sufficiently detail the weighted selection (specifying entries by wage level I–IV); it is unclear what 'caps' commenters meant; DHS notes it is not legally required to publish such information but already makes certain annual information public and will consider what additional information, if any, to make publicly available beyond annual reports and the H-1B Data Hub.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency expectations include publication of clear regulatory text specifying weighting (e.g., entries per wage level) and stakeholders can request further technical guidance or data, but DHS views publication of selection outcomes as discretionary (not legally required) and will weigh operational/privacy/legal constraints before releasing additional datasets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic wage-difference guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters requested clear guidance on how geographic wage differences will be handled in the weighted-selection process. DHS response: LCA/OEWS-based wage levels (occupation and geography specific) are used to assign wage levels; wage-level assignments are codified in regulation (entries per wage level).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing the rule, check that wage-level assignments are derived from OEWS/LCA geography-specific wage estimates and that the rule's text explains how geographic differentials map to wage levels for selection weighting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence requirement before adding weighted selection (prematurity argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters argued weighted selection is premature without a transparent assessment of FY 2025–FY 2026 outcomes under the beneficiary-centric rule and evidence of 'material integrity gaps' that weighting would fix. DHS response: beneficiary-centric selection and weighted selection serve different, complementary policy goals; it is appropriate to have both and no evidence was provided that beneficiary-centric measures obviate the need for weighting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy changes that alter selection probabilities should be justified by policy goals (e.g., prioritize higher-skilled/high-paid beneficiaries) and may be implemented without waiting for long-term outcome studies if agency finds complementary goals and compelling policy directives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of Presidential directives and parallel policies (Proclamation interplay)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters asked DHS to consider the combined effect of the rule and Presidential Proclamation (e.g., $100,000 fee), warning of pricing out small entities and deterring international students/workers. DHS response: the rule is consistent with the Proclamation's direction to prioritize high-skilled/high-paid aliens; the Proclamation does not apply to all petitions, may grant exceptions, expires after 12 months, and is distinct from this rule which applies to all cap-subject petitions and continues indefinitely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a new regulation is consistent with other executive actions and whether differences in scope, duration, and applicability meaningfully change expected combined impacts; DHS treats the rule as complementary, not redundant, to the Proclamation.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA comment-period adequacy (30 vs 60 days)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters requested a 30-day extension to a 60-day comment period under E.O.s 12866 and 13563 citing economic significance and complexity. DHS response: 30 days was sufficient given (1) the narrow scope of the rulemaking (selection process only) and (2) the history of rulemaking on the topic; DHS has a compelling policy interest and a Presidential directive to move expeditiously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency should justify short comment periods by articulating narrow scope, prior notice/history, and compelling policy directives; stakeholders may cite EO guidance recommending 60 days for economically significant rules, but DHS’s stated standard is that 30 days suffices when scope is narrow and prior notice exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision not to delay implementation or republish supplemental NPRM
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters urged DHS to publish a supplemental NPRM or delay implementation until FY 2028 to address perceived shortcomings (e.g., deterrence of hiring for hard-to-fill roles, offshore incentives, variable compensation, exemptions for critical infrastructure, clarifying relocations/multiple locations/SOC flexibility). DHS response: declines to delay or republish; believes weighted methodology balances policy goals and administrability and is implementable for FY 2027.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether to delay implementation, consider whether the selected methodology reasonably balances policy objectives and administrability and whether outstanding issues materially undermine fairness or operability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Flexibility Analysis focus and small-entity impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters claimed the RIA failed to address impacts on small businesses, which are primary job creators and could be priced out. DHS response: acknowledges potential significant impacts on small entities but states impacts reflect distributional outcomes of administering a fixed statutory cap (not new compliance costs); carve-outs for small businesses would be inconsistent with policy objectives; IRFA addressed affected small entities and alternatives, so reopening comment period is not warranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RFA/IRFA analyses should (a) quantify direct impacts on small entities where data permit, (b) explain whether impacts are distributional versus new compliance costs, and (c justify rejecting carve-outs when inconsistent with policy objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of LCA wage data as a proxy for registration wage data
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters argued using LCA wage data is ambiguous because LCAs are not required at registration and registration-level wage choices may differ. DHS response: LCAs are not required at registration and registrations do not include verified wage-level information; LCAs validated at petition stage provide a reliable basis, and for analytical purposes DHS assumes petition (LCA) wage distributions reasonably approximate registration distributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When registration-stage wage data are unavailable, use validated petition-stage LCA wage data as a reasonable proxy, and explicitly state the proxy assumption, its limitations, and the direction of potential bias (e.g., proffered wages exceeding LCA wages would make projections upper bounds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of economic assessment (no obligation to model indirect/secondary effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: A commenter said DHS failed to model broader economic costs (e.g., distortions, disparate geographic impacts). DHS response: RFA does not require assessment of indirect/secondary effects; IRFA/FRFA focus on direct economic impacts on small entities subject to the selection process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory analyses under the RFA should focus on direct impacts required by statute; agencies may decline to model broader economy-wide or indirect effects if not required, but should acknowledge stakeholder concerns and explain scope limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling methodology: without-replacement selection requires simulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters alleged calculation errors and misuse of with-replacement probability multiplications. DHS response: selection is without replacement (unique beneficiaries can be selected only once), so multiplying number of petitions by selection probability assumes with-replacement and overstates selections; calculating weighted probability without replacement is intractable, so DHS used Monte Carlo simulation to estimate results (Table 13).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For lotteries/selection systems conducted without replacement, analytic weighted-probability multiplications can be misleading; use simulation methods (e.g., Monte Carlo) and explain why simulation is necessary and how results were produced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of unique beneficiaries and inability to merge registrations with LCAs
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters said DHS relied on petitions (winners) instead of registrations and could merge registrations with LCAs; DHS response: DHS does not have information to merge registrations with LCAs because LCAs are not required at registration and many registrations never mature into petitions; beneficiary-centric selection reduced duplicate registrations and the rule assigns the lowest wage level across multiple registrations to prevent gaming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should acknowledge data limitations at the registration stage, justify use of petition/LCA data, and explain operational rules (e.g., lowest wage level governs selection probability for beneficiaries with multiple registrations) that mitigate gaming incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pooling modeling choice for regular cap and advanced degree exemption
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters argued DHS combined the regular cap and advanced degree exemption in modeling despite different wage-level distributions and two-step selection for advanced-degree beneficiaries. DHS response: pooled draw modeling is more tractable and results in only a small loss of accuracy because the advanced-degree pool is 20,000 of 85,000 slots and wage-level mixes are broadly similar; the difference between pooled and two-step models is minor relative to weighting effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When two-step selection structures exist, agencies may adopt pooled-draw models for tractability if they demonstrate the approximation error is small and explain the tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wages as a proxy for skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters argued wage level is not the same as skill and the NPRM does not show weighting will raise skill or pay. DHS response: wages reflect market valuation of skills and productivity; OEWS-derived wage levels capture occupation- and geography-specific conditions and are a reasonable proxy for progressively higher skill; weighting is intended to encourage employers to offer higher wages and thus increase selected high-wage hires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies relying on wages as proxies for skill should (a) justify the proxy by citing data sources and economic rationale (e.g., OEWS), (b) acknowledge limitations, and (c explain the intended behavioral effect of weighting on employer wage offers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory/data disclosure obligations (ACWIA and public reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS notes it already makes annual information public pursuant to ACWIA (e.g., countries of origin, occupations, education levels, compensation) via an annual report to Congress and the H-1B Data Hub; DHS will consider what additional information may be appropriate to make publicly available beyond these sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When stakeholders request data publication, identify legal reporting obligations already met (e.g., ACWIA) and describe ongoing monitoring and discretionary data-release considerations, including privacy and operational constraints.
